title: Is your phone distracting you when you're not using it?

source.citation: Ward, A. F., Duke, K., Gneezy, A., & Bos, M. W. (2017). Brain drain: The mere presence of one's own smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 2(2), 140-154. Second study cited: Stothart, C., Mitchum, A., & Yehnert, C. (2015). The attentional cost of receiving a cell phone notification. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance, 41(4), 893-897.
source.finding: Ward et al. reported lower scores on thinking tests when participants' phones were on the desk rather than in another room. Stothart et al. reported that receiving a notification, without responding to it, increased errors on an attention task.
source.caveat: The 'brain drain' result is disputed: a pre-registered replication (Ruiz Pardo & Minda, 2022, Acta Psychologica) did not find it, and meta-analyses disagree about whether the effect exists and how big it is. The notification study is a single experiment. The script says this out loud.

scenes.narration: Your phone might be distracting you even when you're not touching it.
In a 2017 study, people did worse on thinking tests with their phone on the desk. Even switched off.
But be careful. Other researchers repeated it and often found nothing. The evidence is mixed.
A separate 2015 study found that just getting a notification hurt focus. Even when people ignored it.
So nobody can promise your phone drains your brain. But a buzzing one probably isn't helping.
Today, for one study session, put your phone on silent in another room. See if you notice.
